A snowball is rolling down a snow-covered hillside so that its volume increases at a rate of $40\pi \,{\text{in}}^{3}\text{/s}.$ How fast is the radius of the snowball increasing at the moment when the radius is $2.5\,\text{in}$ in length?
question.worked_solution:
Let $r$ be the radius of the balloon and $V$ its volume. Both $r$ and $V$ change with time. In particular, we are given

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=40\pi \,{\text{in}}^{3}/\text{s},
$$

and we want to find $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}$ when $r=2.5\,\text{in}.$

To start, let's write down the volume formula for the sphere and then differentiate it using implicit differentiation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(V) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}r}(\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 4\pi {r}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now we can substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=40\pi $ and $r=2.5,$ and solve for $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}40\pi  & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 4\pi (2.5)^{2} \\ 40\pi  & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 25\pi  \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =1.6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of the snowball is increasing at a rate of $1.6\,\text{in}/\text{s}$ when the radius is $2.5\,\text{in}.$
